lesson.title: ob: Whether or Not
lesson.subtitle: the indirect yes/no word — and the true twin of English if

hook.title: Two Ifs, One Ancient Word
hook.content: German has two ifs and refuses to share. wenn runs the conditions (if it rains...). ob handles the open question folded inside a statement: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt — I don't know IF he is coming. And here is the family secret: ob is the true twin of English if. Both descend from Proto-Germanic *jabai — English wore it down to if, German to ob, same ancient word, same job of opening a yes/no question inside a bigger sentence. English meanwhile drafted whether for the job German gives ob — and whether literally means 'which of the two', which is exactly what ob asks: yes, or no?

footnotes.title: The 'Or Not' Test
footnotes.content: Not sure whether to use ob or wenn? Try adding 'or not'. I don't know if he's coming... or not → works → German wants ob. IF it rains... or not → breaks the sentence → German wants wenn. Ob reports an unanswered yes/no; wenn builds a condition on it.

pattern.title: ob in the Basement
pattern.content: The frames: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt (I don't know whether he is coming). Ich weiß nicht, ob er Zeit hat (whether he has time — hat, haben's fortress form). Wir sehen, ob es regnet (we'll see whether it's raining). Ich möchte wissen, ob du kommst (I would like to know whether you are coming — möchte back from the escalator). Contrast pair: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt (whether — open question) versus Wenn er kommt, lese ich (if — condition). Both are basement clauses — the verb waits at the end for ob exactly as for wenn, weil and dass.
pattern.linguist_note: Proto-Germanic *jabai ('when, if') forked into English if and German ob — one of the rare pairs where the English twin looks NOTHING like its German sibling until the pedigree is on the table. The b and the f are the same ancient labial consonant, voiced differently down the centuries.

exercises.prompt: The two ifs — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: I don't know whether he is coming
matching_pairs.german: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt

matching_pairs.english: I don't know whether my friend is coming
matching_pairs.german: Ich weiß nicht, ob mein Freund kommt

exercises.target_answer: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt, Wenn es regnet, lese ich, ob sie Zeit hat, Wenn ich Zeit hätte, Ich weiß nicht, ob mein Freund kommt
exercises.meaning: ob for open questions, wenn for conditions
exercises.explanation: ob reports an open yes/no; wenn builds a condition. English splits the same jobs between whether/if and if.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich weiß nicht, _____ er kommt.' (I don't know IF/WHETHER...):
exercises.meaning: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt
exercises.explanation: The 'or not' test: 'whether he is coming or not' works → ob. An indirect yes/no question folds ob into the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Choose the conditional subordinator: '_____ du kommst, lese ich.' (If/whenever you come, I read):
exercises.meaning: Wenn du kommst, lese ich = if you come, I read
exercises.explanation: A condition built on the other clause's action → wenn. ob cannot build conditions — it only reports open questions.

exercises.prompt: ob looks nothing like it — but which everyday English word is its true twin (Proto-Germanic *jabai)?
exercises.explanation: English if and German ob both descend from *jabai. The family resemblance hid for a thousand years; the pedigree exposes it.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the German sentence you hear:
exercises.target_answer: Ich weiß nicht ob er Zeit hat
exercises.meaning: Ich weiß nicht, ob er Zeit hat

vocab_hints.note: the indirect yes/no word — verb goes to the basement

exercises.explanation: weiß holds position 2 of the main clause; hat waits at the basement end — ob's clause runs on weil's rules.
exercises.spoken: Ich weiß nicht ob er Zeit hat
cues: Meaning: "Ich weiß nicht, ob er Zeit hat"
Opens with "Ich weiß" and ends with "hat".

summary.outcome: Use ob for indirect yes/no questions, contrast it with wenn, and name English if as its twin.

use_example.german: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt — wenn er kommt, lese ich.
use_example.english: I don't know whether he's coming — if he comes, I'll read.

summary.takeaway: ob asks the open yes/no ('or not' test), wenn builds the condition — and ob is English if, disguised.
summary.curiosity_teaser: This whether-branch ends here — more side paths wait on the map, and the whole compendium waits in review.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from ob: Whether or Not (Ich weiß nicht, ob er Zeit hat):
twist.target_answer: Ich weiß nicht ob er Zeit hat
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich weiß nicht ob er Zeit hat" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of ob: Whether or Not without relying on short-term echo.

ob.context_phrase: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt.
ob.context_translation: I do not know whether he is coming.
ob.etymology_derivation: From Old High German oba, from Proto-Germanic *jabai 'when, if' — the true cognate of English if (both carry the same ancient labial). [wiktionary]

wenn.context_phrase: Wenn ich Zeit habe, lese ich.
wenn.context_translation: When(ever) I have time, I read.
wenn.etymology_derivation: Old High German hwanne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan — the exact twin of English when and the etymological doublet of German wann: wann asks the question, wenn builds the clause. [wiktionary]

mögen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "may" and "might" (Proto-Germanic *maganą). Subjunctive: möchte (would like).

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

freund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, 'the loving one' — the exact twin of English friend. [wiktionary]

haar.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hār — the same word as English hair. [wiktionary]

abendessen.context_phrase: Das Abendessen ist um acht Uhr.
abendessen.etymology_derivation: Abend (evening) + Essen (meal) — a transparent compound of known parts. [wiktionary]

müsli.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Alemannic Muesli, a diminutive of Mus, meaning porridge; Mus is cognate with English mush, and English borrowed the word muesli from German. [wiktionary]

schlimm.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slimbaz 'crooked, oblique' — the page lists English slim as a cognate; schlimm slid from crooked to bad, and Middle Dutch slim also meant bad. [wiktionary]

hungrig.context_phrase: Die Kinder sind hungrig nach der Schule.
hungrig.context_translation: The children are hungry after school.
hungrig.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hungrugaz, by surface analysis Hunger plus -ig. English hungry is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

autor.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from New Latin autor, from Latin auctor - compare English author and French auteur, all the same word. [wiktionary]

weste.context_phrase: Im Winter trage ich eine Weste.
weste.context_translation: In winter I wear a vest.
weste.etymology_derivation: From French veste (17th century), from Latin vestis, garment — the same French word that gave English vest. [wiktionary]
